screening_decisions.reason: Systematic review evaluating the CFIR in low- and middle-income countries with a quantitative focus on birth-attendant coaching; not a primary qualitative study and not about home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with caregivers and staff to explore experiences of rehabilitation-in-the-home programmes and the shifting burden of care from hospital to home.
Framework development paper describing the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research; not about home-based rehabilitation.
Action research project using individual qualitative interviews with staff to develop a model for organisation of and cooperation on home-based rehabilitation in two boroughs.

Protocol for a qualitative study on eHealth ethics and multimorbidity; not a completed study and not specifically about home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative study using video recordings and individual interviews to explore how support personnel practice in Norwegian reablement services, which are home-based rehabilitation services supervised by physiotherapists.
Qualitative study developing an international classification system for rehabilitation service organisation generally; not specifically about home-based rehabilitation.
Pilot case series of telerehabilitation for traumatic brain injury using quantitative outcome measures and descriptive statistics; not a qualitative study.
Cochrane review of telerehabilitation for people with low vision; no completed trials included and not a qualitative study.

Non-randomized open trial of a care coordination home-telehealth programme for stroke recovery; focus is on care coordination, depression and falls rather than rehabilitation service provision, and the qualitative component is not clearly described as the primary methodology.
Qualitative study exploring experiences of a web-based nursing intervention for women with chronic musculoskeletal pain; nursing intervention, not rehabilitation.

Qualitative study (phenomenological-hermeneutic interviews and narrative analysis) exploring patient experiences of a cardiac tele-rehabilitation program delivered remotely at home. Directly addresses home-based telerehabilitation and patient perceptions.
Report of a WHO policy event and call to action; not a primary qualitative study collecting data on stakeholders' experiences of home-based rehabilitation services.

Qualitative study using nested one-on-one interviews and thematic analysis to explore stroke patients' experiences of traditional home exercise programs and acceptability of a novel home-based intervention. Relevant to in-person home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative study focused on transition experiences from hospital to home after an inpatient outreach program. The primary focus is transition expectations rather than the organisation, delivery, or provision of home-based rehabilitation services.

Mixed-methods process evaluation including qualitative interviews and document analysis exploring barriers and facilitators to implementing a home-based cardiac rehabilitation program. Directly addresses factors influencing the provision of home-based rehabilitation. Qualitative phenomenological study of general home care after burn injury discharge. While rehabilitation is mentioned broadly, the focus is on home nursing and healing rather than structured home-based rehabilitation service provision.

Qualitative study examining why informal family caregivers provide rehabilitation at home. The review focuses on formal home-based rehabilitation services and their organisation/delivery; informal caregiving by relatives falls outside the scope of professional service provision.

Qualitative study exploring clinician perceptions of a specific wearable technology prototype. The focus is device acceptability and technical implementation rather than the broader organisation and delivery of home-based rehabilitation services.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of effectiveness; not a primary qualitative study using qualitative methods for data collection and analysis of experiences/perceptions.

Qualitative study examining a nurse's advice within a web-based supportive intervention for caregivers. The intervention is educational/supportive rather than home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation, and the analysis focuses on nurse responses rather than service delivery factors.

Qualitative case study using focus groups, interviews, document analysis and video recordings to explore how telerehabilitation is integrated into routine practice for traumatic brain and spinal cord injury patients. Identifies factors enabling or constraining routine use, directly relevant to home-based telerehabilitation provision.

Mixed-methods pilot evaluating accessibility and user-friendliness of a specific digital self-management resource. Focused on product development and refinement rather than exploring factors influencing the organisation and delivery of home-based rehabilitation services.

Qualitative interview study using content analysis to explore patients' experiences of video-based physiotherapy telerehabilitation delivered at home after shoulder joint replacement. Directly addresses home-based telerehabilitation and patient experiences.

Mixed-methods pilot including qualitative evaluation (focus groups and interviews) exploring patient perceptions of an online cardiac rehabilitation programme used at home. Addresses patient experiences of a home-based telerehabilitation intervention.

Convergent parallel mixed-methods design with extensive qualitative data (22 interviews, document analysis) analysed using CFIR to identify barriers and facilitators to implementing a home-based cardiac rehabilitation program. Directly addresses factors influencing the organisation and delivery of home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative study exploring mobility outcome preferences during post-acute inpatient or skilled nursing facility rehabilitation. The setting and focus are inpatient care and outcome preferences, not home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation service provision.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of effectiveness; not a primary qualitative study of experiences/perceptions.

Mixed-methods development study using focus groups and think-aloud interviews to establish design requirements for a web-based exercise program. Focused on intervention development and usability rather than experiences of receiving or organising home-based rehabilitation services.
Methodological paper about the GRADE-CERQual approach; not a primary qualitative study of home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative focus group study exploring preferences for physical activity information delivery channels. The focus is health information dissemination, not the organisation, delivery, or experiences of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.
Narrative review categorising types of home-based rehabilitation programs. Not a primary qualitative study with original qualitative data collection and analysis.
Protocol for a Cochrane qualitative evidence synthesis on physical activity for bipolar disorder. Not a completed primary study and the topic is not home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative study using interviews with patients and staff to explore experiences and obstacles affecting choice between home-based and hospital-based cardiac rehabilitation. Identifies systems-level and practical factors influencing the provision of home-based rehabilitation (e.g., referral, information, resources).
Cochrane review of early discharge hospital-at-home services; not a primary qualitative study. Also focuses on acute hospital-at-home alternatives rather than rehabilitation service provision.

Qualitative study using repeated interviews and grounded theory to explore older adults' experiences and perceptions of staff during six months of home-based rehabilitation. Directly addresses stakeholder experiences of in-person home-based rehabilitation provision.

Mixed-methods usability study of a mobile exercise application. Focused on technology usability, effectiveness, and ease of use rather than the organisation and delivery of home-based rehabilitation services.
Cochrane review assessing effects of home-based survivorship programmes; not a primary qualitative study.

Qualitative interview study exploring stroke patients' expectations of very early supported discharge and home rehabilitation after stroke. Directly relevant to in-person home-based rehabilitation. Note: the supplied abstract is mismatched (appears to be from a neurocysticercosis case report), but the title clearly indicates a qualitative study of home-based stroke rehabilitation.

Qualitative study exploring reasons for nonattendance at Phase III outpatient cardiac rehabilitation programmes. The setting is outpatient/hospital-based programmes, not home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation.
Narrative overview chapter discussing telerehabilitation technologies and presenting case studies. Not a primary qualitative research study with systematic qualitative data collection and analysis.
Systematic review comparing inpatient and home-based rehabilitation outcomes; not a primary qualitative study.

Primarily a quantitative crossover trial measuring clinical outcomes (motivation, physical activity, glycated hemoglobin). Although some qualitative data were collected, the abstract does not describe a qualitative analytical approach or report qualitative findings related to the provision of home-based rehabilitation services.

Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with patients and practitioners, analyzed thematically. It explicitly explores experiences of a videoconferencing (telerehabilitation) care model for chronic back disorders, identifying access, interprofessional practice and technology considerations relevant to service delivery.

The provided abstract describes a cross-sectional survey of private practitioners regarding tuberculosis notification in India; it is unrelated to home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation and does not employ qualitative methods relevant to this review.

Mixed-methods study with a primary qualitative component (semi-structured interviews at baseline and 3 months) seeking to identify barriers and facilitators to a home-based cycling intervention. It captures patient experiences of a home-based rehabilitation program and is therefore relevant.

Qualitative focus-group study involving stroke patients, informal caregivers and healthcare professionals. It explores influencing factors and stakeholder experiences of eRehabilitation (telerehabilitation) uptake, directly addressing factors that affect service organisation and delivery.

The provided abstract reports a cross-sectional study of a robotic Trunk-Support-Trainer device for spinal cord injury. It does not concern home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation service provision and lacks a qualitative design.

Longitudinal qualitative study using repeated semi-structured interviews and inductive thematic analysis to explore older adults’ ongoing experiences of internet-guided, self-managed vestibular rehabilitation delivered at home. Clearly relevant to home-based telerehabilitation.
This is a meeting report/copyright notice, not a primary empirical study, and contains no qualitative data on home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative study employing a user-centred design process with community-dwelling brain-injured adults and therapists. It explores experiences and perspectives of a remote, home-based cognitive rehabilitation application, fitting the review’s scope.

The study relies on an End of Study Questionnaire and content analysis of responses to a post-chemotherapy lifestyle intervention. It is not clearly a rehabilitation service, the method is primarily survey-based, and the abstract does not demonstrate in-depth qualitative data collection and analysis.

Qualitative findings drawn from therapist telephone interviews, technical support documentation and a post-study debriefing, analyzed thematically. The study identifies factors influencing the use of a home-based virtual rehabilitation system from the perspectives of therapists, engineers and users.

Qualitative interview study using content analysis linked to the ICF environmental domain. It explicitly explores facilitators and barriers influencing activity and participation among older people receiving home rehabilitation, directly relevant to factors affecting service delivery.

Realist evaluation incorporating focus groups, home visits and in-depth case studies with stroke survivors and caregivers. It generates and tests context-mechanism-outcome configurations for a home-based technology-enhanced rehabilitation system, yielding qualitative insights into what influences home-based service delivery.

The provided abstract describes a quantitative survey (KORA-Age) comparing self-reported health-care utilization with official statistics. It is not a qualitative focus group study, does not address home-based rehabilitation service provision, and the title/abstract mismatch prevents confirmation of relevance.

Qualitative interview study using inductive thematic analysis to examine how stroke patients and caregivers experience home-based caregiver-mediated exercises. It addresses patient and caregiver experiences of a home-based rehabilitation approach.

Qualitative focus-group study using constructivist grounded theory. It explores health professionals’ perspectives on collaborating with next of kin during reablement, a time-limited, home-based rehabilitation-like intervention, making it directly relevant.

Mixed-methods formative study that includes ethnographic semi-structured patient interviews and key-informant interviews with clinicians. The qualitative component explores end-user needs, preferences and priorities for a mobile pulmonary rehabilitation support program (home-based telerehabilitation).

Qualitative extension of a feasibility trial, using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis to capture experiences of persons with MS who participated in a home-based exercise program. It provides patient perspectives on home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative interview study guided by phenomenological methodology exploring older people’s lived experiences of rehabilitation in their own homes after total hip replacement. It directly addresses home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative study using focus groups with breast cancer patients to identify user needs and requirements for a mobile app supporting home-based exercise after treatment. It explores patient experiences and preferences for home-based telerehabilitation.

Qualitative interview study exploring mild-stroke survivors’ experiences of rehabilitation delivered in their homes during early supported discharge. It captures patient experiences of home-based stroke rehabilitation.

This is a Cochrane systematic review of randomized controlled trials of telerehabilitation in stroke. It is not a primary qualitative study and does not report qualitative data collection or analysis.

Qualitative study using interviews with care professionals and non-participatory observations, analyzed with content analysis and modelling. It examines interaction points in post-discharge stroke care and rehabilitation, illuminating how patients, next-of-kin and professionals collaborate in home-based care.

Although it uses self-reported qualitative data, the study focuses on barriers to community reintegration (mobility, insurance, environment) after discharge, not on the provision or delivery of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.

Qualitative case study using interviews and participant observation in patients’ homes to explore attitudes toward tele-rehabilitation. It directly addresses patient experiences of a home-based telerehabilitation program.

Case study incorporating telephone interviews with patients recovering from acute coronary syndrome about a home-based cardiac rehabilitation program. The interview component yields qualitative perspectives on service structures and processes, relevant to factors influencing provision.

Qualitative interview study exploring usability and experiences of a 14-week home-based Wii Fit exercise program among adults with multiple sclerosis. It provides user perspectives on a home-based rehabilitation intervention.

Qualitative interview study using content analysis to explore older adults’ experiences and driving forces in home-based reablement. It directly addresses factors influencing a home-based rehabilitation intervention.

Primarily a randomized controlled pilot trial assessing effectiveness of web-based physiotherapy. The qualitative component (website evaluation and interviews) is minor, not described in detail, and the abstract emphasizes quantitative efficacy outcomes rather than qualitative analysis of service provision.

Descriptive exploratory qualitative study using semi-structured interviews to explore how older people manage home rehabilitation after orthopaedic surgery. It directly addresses experiences and factors influencing home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative interview study exploring patient experiences of a virtual, home-based cardiac rehabilitation program. It identifies barriers and facilitators (e.g., access, accountability, computer literacy) relevant to home-based telerehabilitation.

The study is a cross-sectional quantitative investigation of arterial stiffness parameters (AASI/HASI) in hypertensive patients. It employs no qualitative methods for data collection or analysis and does not address home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation provision.

This mixed-methods study uses qualitative staff observations and documentary analysis to examine technology support for a telehealth-in-the-home trial that included home-based rehabilitation services for the elderly. It explores clinicians’ and technical stakeholders’ experiences, workflow embedding, usability, and training needs—factors directly influencing the delivery of home-based telerehabilitation.

This is a scoping review summarising effectiveness evidence of home-based rehabilitation interventions for adults living with HIV. It is not a primary qualitative study and therefore does not meet the inclusion criteria.

A structured methodological review on searching for qualitative research for systematic reviews. The topic is information retrieval methodology, not the organisation or delivery of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.

Qualitative focus groups with patients and health care professionals were used to identify critical features of pulmonary telerehabilitation. The study explicitly explores stakeholders’ perceptions and experiences regarding the provision of telehealth-delivered rehabilitation, aligning with the review’s objective and qualitative inclusion criteria.

Although the overall design includes a prospective cohort, the study incorporates qualitative analysis of interviews to investigate patients’ experiences, barriers, and facilitators when using a home-based virtual reality rehabilitation system after stroke. This yields experiential data relevant to factors affecting the provision of home-based rehabilitation.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials evaluating physical function outcomes after home-based rehabilitation post-stroke. It is not a primary qualitative study and does not provide qualitative data on experiences or perceptions.

This is a Cochrane review protocol/article assessing the effectiveness and safety of telerehabilitation for persons with multiple sclerosis. As a review of effectiveness, it is not a primary qualitative study.

A state-of-the-art review of telerehabilitation applications. It synthesises existing literature rather than reporting primary qualitative research on stakeholders’ experiences of home-based rehabilitation service provision.

The article is a commentary/letter concerning teleophthalmology (remote eye care) and the concept of medical virtualists. It does not address home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation, nor does it report qualitative methods.

Qualitative design using focus group interviews with members of a newly established multidisciplinary team delivering home-based everyday rehabilitation. The study explores team members’ experiences with developing a collaborative work model, revealing organisational and interpersonal factors that influence the delivery of in-person home-based rehabilitation.

An action research project collecting qualitative data via individual and group interviews with front-line service providers and managers in home-based services. It examines how rehabilitation work is perceived and practised in the home setting, identifying system-level and resource-related factors influencing provision.

Qualitative semi-structured interviews with physiotherapists practising home-based stroke rehabilitation. The study investigates the content of rehabilitation delivered in patients’ homes and the clinical reasoning behind practice decisions, offering direct insight into provider-level factors affecting in-person home-based rehabilitation.

Interviews with clients who received an individualised, multidisciplinary home-based rehabilitation programme after stroke. Thematic analysis of client experiences generates qualitative evidence on patient perspectives, goal-setting, and the role of the home environment in rehabilitation delivery.

A mixed-methods study exploring needs for mobile health solutions to support physical activity in persons with multiple sclerosis. While it involves qualitative components, the focus is on physical activity apps rather than the provision of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.

Qualitative case study of a cardiac telerehabilitation programme using document analysis, participant observation, and interviews with health care professionals across sectors. It explores interorganisational cooperation, workflow integration, and unification of organisations—key factors influencing the delivery of home-based telerehabilitation.

Qualitative content analysis of narratives provided by community-based occupational therapists describing ethical dilemmas encountered during rehabilitation in home care settings. The study captures therapists’ experiences and contextual challenges inherent to the provision of home-based rehabilitation.

The abstract describes a community-based paediatric hearing screening programme using tele-medicine, which does not correspond to the title and is unrelated to home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation for people needing rehabilitation. No qualitative evidence on rehabilitation provision is present.

A qualitative study on caregiver needs in heart failure management intended to inform a home-based self-management resource. Although the intervention is home-based, the focus is self-management rather than rehabilitation service provision, and participants’ experiences centre on caregiving for heart failure, not on home-based rehab or telerehab.

Qualitative embedded case study using semi-structured interviews with patients who received in-home telerehabilitation physiotherapy after total knee arthroplasty. It explores patient perceptions of access, therapeutic relationships, exercise delivery, and support, directly addressing experiences of home-based telerehabilitation provision.

This study examines the acceptability of real-time videoconferencing for follow-up consultations in shoulder instability. The focus is on a single remote clinical consultation rather than on the organisation or delivery of a home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation programme, and it does not explore rehabilitation experiences.

Focus groups and interviews with stroke survivors explore perceptions of person-generated health data from a simulated (sham) rehabilitation technology. The study does not address the provision of actual home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services, nor is the setting clearly home-based.

The title indicates a qualitative focus group study aimed at identifying end-user requirements for eRehabilitation programs in stroke care—an area that falls within home-based telerehabilitation. Because the provided abstract is mismatched (it discusses clinical text classification), certainty is reduced; however, applying a conservative approach, the study is retained for full-text review given its explicit alignment with the review topic in the title.

Qualitative interviews with clinicians investigate patient involvement in goal-setting during stroke rehabilitation. While two teams are community-based, the study does not specifically examine the provision of in-person home-based rehabilitation or home-based telerehabilitation services, focusing instead on goal-setting processes across inpatient and community settings.

A brief commentary or overview article describing the concept and aims of home rehabilitation. It does not report primary qualitative research or present data on stakeholders’ experiences, perceptions, or behaviours.

Semi-structured interviews with patients who completed a home-based rehabilitation programme for inoperable lung cancer. The study elicits patient experiences, benefits, barriers, and facilitators, yielding qualitative evidence on factors influencing the delivery and uptake of home-based rehabilitation.

A feasibility and usability study of a web-based application (TRAK app) for knee rehabilitation. Although stakeholders were consulted, the study is primarily a technical usability evaluation using questionnaires and does not constitute a primary qualitative investigation of experiences regarding home-based rehabilitation service provision.

Qualitative retrospective interviews with members of a multiprofessional team using the Empirical Phenomenological Psychological method. The study explores the meaning of rehabilitation in the home environment after acute stroke, revealing team perceptions of continuity, patient functioning, and contextual factors that shape in-person home-based rehabilitation delivery.

The title suggests a home telehealth project, but the provided abstract discusses community-based health insurance and healthcare-seeking behaviour in rural India, with no mention of rehabilitation or qualitative data on rehab service provision. Consequently, it does not meet the inclusion criteria.

A mixed-methods evaluation incorporating semi-structured interviews with patients and home care clinicians about an adapted cardiac rehabilitation programme delivered in the home care setting. The qualitative component captures experiences and perceptions of feasibility and acceptability, providing evidence on factors influencing home-based rehabilitation provision.
Qualitative study interviewing patients about a home-based cardiac rehabilitation programme; explores patient perceptions and experiences of home-based rehab. Meets inclusion criteria.

Case report evaluating telerehabilitation via remote presence robot for a single patient; includes only one semi-structured interview and a satisfaction survey. Not a primary qualitative study and does not meet the requirement for qualitative methods as the primary design.
Systematic rapid living review collating evidence on rehabilitation needs due to COVID-19; not a primary qualitative study.

Qualitative interpretative phenomenological analysis of semi-structured interviews exploring experiences of home-based computerized cognitive training and the therapeutic alliance. Concerns home-based cognitive rehabilitation and stakeholder experiences.

Mixed-methods case study including in-depth interviews with key informants about rehabilitation home-care service provision under managed competition; captures stakeholder perspectives on delivery of home-based rehab services. Qualitative component meets criteria.
Systematic review of randomized controlled trials on home-based rehabilitation effectiveness; not a primary qualitative study.
Qualitative study using interviews with patients and partners about early supported discharge and rehabilitation at home; directly explores experiences of home-based stroke rehabilitation.
Cochrane rapid living systematic review of rehabilitation and COVID-19; not a primary qualitative study.

Qualitative research using semi-structured interviews with acquired brain injury patients and caregivers about service and support needs during transition from hospital to home; explores perceptions of rehabilitation services in the home context.

Action research trial of home telehealth video conferencing with emphasis on technical performance metrics and quantitative clinician ratings; not a primary qualitative study and lacks clear qualitative analysis of experiences as the main focus.
Systematic review of barriers and facilitators to rehabilitation services; not a primary qualitative study.
Observational feasibility study of a smartphone application in cardiac rehabilitation with quantitative task tracking and mixed feedback; not a primary qualitative study.
Conceptual article proposing a fourth factor for evidence-based decision-making in rehabilitation; does not report primary qualitative data on home-based rehabilitation provision.

Pilot feasibility randomised controlled trial of a home-based prevention programme after TIA/minor stroke; primary design is quantitative and the qualitative component (focus groups) is secondary and limited. Does not meet criteria for a primary qualitative study.

Qualitative exploration using semi-structured interviews with cardiovascular disease patients and health professionals about requirements for a home-based eHealth cardiac rehabilitation intervention; explores stakeholder experiences and needs for home-based telerehabilitation.

Qualitative study using focus groups and thematic analysis with hospital-based therapists about an approach providing therapy sessions in the home/community before discharge; explores health provider experiences of home-based rehabilitation provision.

Qualitative study using interpretative phenomenological analysis of patient interviews about choosing home-based versus hospital-based cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction; directly explores patient experiences and perceptions of home-based rehab.

Pilot descriptive study of an Internet-based support intervention for rural caregivers of stroke survivors; focuses on caregiver support and experience of caring rather than on the provision of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.
Global Burden of Disease systematic analysis estimating rehabilitation need; epidemiological secondary data analysis, not a primary qualitative study.

Ethnographic fieldwork exploring telemediated exercise training delivered at home for patients with severe COPD and their partners; uses qualitative methods to examine experiences of home-based telerehabilitation in everyday life.
Commentary on maintaining rehabilitation services during COVID-19; not a primary qualitative study.

Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis to report patient perspectives on home-based pulmonary rehabilitation; directly explores experiences of a home-based rehabilitation programme.
White Book chapter providing an overview of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine in healthcare systems; not a primary qualitative study of home-based rehabilitation experiences.

Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis examining female cancer survivors' perspectives on remote monitoring and communication to support physical activity maintenance at home; concerns home-based telerehabilitation/exercise and stakeholder experiences.

The provided abstract describes an interview-based study of general eHealth programmes in India, not home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services; topic mismatch means it does not meet the review's scope.
Systematic rapid living review on rehabilitation needs due to COVID-19; not a primary qualitative study.

Qualitative study using surveys and interviews exploring patients' perspectives on home-based e-Health (telehealth) multidisciplinary service delivery for motor neurone disease; captures patient experiences/perceptions of home-based telerehabilitation.

Phenomenological qualitative study using interpretative phenomenological analysis of interviews about a virtual rehabilitation program used at home after amputation; explores patient bodily experiences of home-based virtual rehabilitation.

Descriptive qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis exploring physiotherapists' perceptions of delivering telephone-based exercise therapy for knee osteoarthritis; directly concerns home-based telerehabilitation and provider experiences.

Participatory action design study focused on developing a wheelchair skills home program; aims at intervention design and validation rather than exploring experiences, perceptions or behaviours about the provision of home-based rehabilitation services.

The study is a randomized controlled trial whose primary analysis is quantitative (caregiver outcome scales). Although qualitative interviews were mentioned, they are not the main data collection/analysis method and no qualitative findings are reported in the abstract.

Qualitative study of ARDS survivors' support needs across the illness trajectory. While it touches on community and home care, it does not specifically explore experiences or perceptions of in-person home-based rehabilitation or home-based telerehabilitation service provision.

Qualitative study using semistructured interviews and a focus group with older adults and health care professionals, analysed via interpretive description. It directly explores experiences and perspectives within a home-based rehabilitation program, aligning with the review objective.

Qualitative interviews explore stroke survivors' place attachment and identity renegotiation. The focus is on spatial and social belonging rather than on the provision or delivery of in-person home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.

Primarily a user-centered design and development study of a telerehabilitation platform. Although qualitative methods (interviews, heuristic evaluation) are used, the aim is platform prototyping and usability rather than exploring stakeholders' experiences of telerehabilitation service provision.

Qualitative study about home care staff experiences with assistive devices. The focus is on devices and their role in daily work, not on the provision of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.

Qualitative analysis of perceived caregiving problems within a web-based intervention project. The focus is on general caregiving challenges rather than on experiences or perceptions of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation service provision.

Grounded theory study exploring significant others' views on ICT in stroke rehabilitation broadly. It does not specifically address home-based telerehabilitation or in-person home-based rehabilitation service delivery.

Qualitative process evaluation of stroke survivors' perceptions of community rehabilitation with/without self-management. Primarily a quantitative feasibility/efficacy study of home-based robotic therapy with quantitative outcomes and brief qualitative surveys. It does not use qualitative methods as the primary data collection and analysis approach.

Pilot evaluation of a specific telepractice application relying mainly on structured questionnaires, with only a small qualitative interview component. The focus is on acceptability of a novel app rather than on factors influencing home-based telerehabilitation service provision broadly.

Development and testing study of a gamification prototype. While some qualitative data collection techniques were used, the primary aim is prototype design and evaluation, not a qualitative exploration of stakeholders' experiences of telerehabilitation provision.

Qualitative study using semistructured individual and focus group interviews with health professionals, analysed using the Theoretical Domains Framework. It directly explores barriers and enablers to online exercise-based telerehabilitation for COPD, fitting the review objective.

Mixed-methods study that includes semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis exploring patient experiences of a group-based heart failure telerehabilitation program delivered to the home via videoconferencing. The qualitative component is substantial and directly relevant to home-based telerehabilitation.
Conceptual discussion paper without empirical qualitative data collection or analysis. It does not meet the qualitative methods inclusion criterion.
Randomized controlled trial comparing home rehabilitation with routine rehabilitation using quantitative outcome measures. No qualitative data collection or analysis is reported.

Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis with stroke patients and carers. It explicitly explores experiences of Early Supported Discharge services, which include home-based rehabilitation, directly addressing the review's focus.

Qualitative study exploring patient participation in a web-based behavior change program combined with multimodal pain rehabilitation. The focus is on participation in a specific web program as part of broader rehabilitation, not specifically on home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation service provision.

Descriptive qualitative study using interviews and phenomenographic analysis with older adults receiving short-term goal-directed reablement at home after hospital discharge. It directly explores older adults' perceptions of home-based reablement, aligning with the review objective.

Qualitative study about user experiences of a mobile educational app for pressure injury prevention. The focus is on education for pressure injury management, not on home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.

User-preference study primarily evaluating a mobile app prototype using quantitative usability scales and brief qualitative feedback. It is not a qualitative study focused on exploring stakeholders' experiences of home-based rehabilitation service provision.

User-centred design study aimed at developing an ICT-based self-management system for home-based stroke rehabilitation. While qualitative methods are used, the primary aim is system development rather than exploring experiences or perceptions of rehabilitation service delivery.
Quantitative secondary data analysis examining adherence to home-based rehabilitation using functional outcome measures. No qualitative methods are employed.
Cochrane systematic review of randomized controlled trials. It is not a primary qualitative study and does not meet the inclusion criteria.

Qualitative study using interviews and systematic text condensation exploring older adults' experiences of participation in daily activities through home-based reablement services. It directly addresses experiences of home-based rehabilitation provision.

Qualitative evaluation of a home-based self-management technology for chronic pain. The focus is on a self-management system rather than on the provision of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.

Qualitative study exploring nurses' perceptions of rehabilitation in long-term residential care homes. The setting is institutional, not patients' own homes, so it does not address home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative study exploring postoperative physiotherapy patient education from the perspective of hospital inpatients after total hip arthroplasty. The focus is on inpatient education rather than on home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation service provision.
Field report summarizing a webinar with association representatives. It lacks systematic qualitative data collection and analysis, and does not meet the qualitative methods inclusion criterion.
Observational cohort study with historical control comparing service volumes and using questionnaires. It does not employ qualitative methods for data collection and analysis.
